questions.stem: What is the function of the myelin sheath?

options.text: To provide nutrients to the neurone
To receive impulses from other neurones
To insulate the axon and speed up impulse transmission
To produce neurotransmitters at the synapse

questions.explanation: The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer around the axon made of Schwann cells. It electrically insulates the axon and allows impulses to jump between gaps (nodes of Ranvier), significantly speeding up transmission.

questions.stem: What are the gaps in the myelin sheath called?
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are regular gaps in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed. These enable saltatory conduction, where the impulse jumps from node to node, greatly increasing the speed of transmission.

questions.stem: Which part of a neurone carries the impulse away from the cell body?
questions.explanation: The axon is a long fibre that carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body towards the axon terminals. In some motor neurones, axons can be up to 1 metre long.

questions.stem: What is the role of dendrites?

options.text: To insulate the axon from surrounding tissue
To release neurotransmitters into the synapse
To carry impulses to the next neurone
To receive impulses from other neurones or receptors

questions.explanation: Dendrites are short branching projections from the cell body that receive impulses from other neurones or from receptors. Their many branches increase the surface area available for receiving signals from multiple sources.

questions.stem: Why do neurones contain many mitochondria?

options.text: To provide energy (ATP) for transmitting nerve impulses

questions.explanation: Neurones contain many mitochondria to carry out aerobic respiration and produce large amounts of ATP. This energy is needed to maintain the resting potential through the sodium-potassium pump and to release neurotransmitters at synapses.

questions.stem: How are impulses transmitted from one neurone to the next across a synapse?

options.text: The axons of the two neurones physically touch
The electrical impulse jumps directly across the gap
Hormones are released into the bloodstream
Chemical neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft

questions.explanation: At a synapse, the electrical impulse triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters from vesicles in the presynaptic neurone. These diffuse across the tiny synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic neurone, triggering a new impulse.

questions.stem: Which type of neurone has its cell body in the middle of the axon?
questions.explanation: Sensory neurones have a distinctive structure where the cell body is located off to the side (in the middle) of the axon, rather than at one end. Motor neurones have their cell body at one end with a long axon extending to the effector.
